messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} \approx 3.2 \text{ V}$.
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nom (Ip=50u, RL=330k)
        *   S2: Heavy load (Ip=50u, RL=150k) -> Fail vavg, tup
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load (Ip=100u, RL=2.2M) -> Fail vmax, vpp, settled
        *   S4: Weak excitation (Ip=30u, RL=1M) -> Fail vavg, tup, settled
        *   S5: Low frequency (Ip=40u, RL=470k) -> Fail settled
        *   S6: Hot, Cp+20% (Ip=50u, RL=330k) -> OK
    *   FBR Results Analysis:
        *   Fails at high loads (S2) and weak excitations (S4) because $V_{oc}$ is too low once diode drops are considered, and it lacks power enhancement.
        *   Fails at light loads (S3) because it overcharges the storage capacitor (no regulation).
        *   Fails settled checks (S1, S3, S5) likely due to $C_{out}$ size or slow approach to equilibrium.

    *   Standard Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) is inefficient for low $V_{oc}$ and cannot regulate.
    *   To improve efficiency (higher $V_{avg}$ for S2, S4):
        *   Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or Parallel-SSHI. SSHI flips the voltage across $C_p$ to increase the harvested energy.
        *   Synchronous Rectification (using switches instead of diodes).
    *   To prevent overvoltage (S3):
        *   Zener clamp (DZ33) on $V_{out}$.
        *   Active regulation (beyond the scope of these components unless we use a SYNC loop cleverly, but SYNC is tied to piezo frequency, not output voltage). A Zener is the easiest way to cap $V_{max}$ at 3.3V.
    *   To reduce ripple and improve settling:
        *   Large storage capacitor $C_{out}$.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI (Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor)*
        *   Basic SSHI uses a switch and an inductor to invert the piezo voltage at peaks.
        *   Circuit: Piezo terminals $pzp, pzn$. An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo? No, typically the inductor and switch create a resonant circuit to flip the voltage.
        *   Actually, a common SSHI is: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage. But *before* the rectifier, a flipping circuit.
        *   Simpler: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).
        *   Let's try a basic SSHI-like inductor flip: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals to invert charge, followed by a rectifier.
        *   Wait, the provided components allow SYNC controllers.
        *   Looking at the reference FBR, it used 4 diodes.
        *   Proposed SSHI: Piezo ($pzp, pzn$) $\to$ Switch $S$ + Inductor $L$ flipping circuit $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        *   Wait, the "L-Cp inversion" is mentioned in the prompt: "For L-Cp inversion, ton is about $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$". This suggests a topology where an inductor is switched across the piezo.
        *   Circuit: $S1$ in parallel with the piezo, but with an inductor $L$ in series? $pzp \to L \to S1 \to pzn$. When $S1$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, flipping the voltage.
        *   After flipping, use a rectifier to move charge to $V_{out}$.

    *   *Topology 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge)*
        *   Replace diodes with switches. However, we only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches. A full bridge needs 4 switches.
        *   If we use 2 SYNCs, we can control 4 switches if we group them. But the prompt says "closes its switches", implying one SYNC can control multiple switches if we give them the same `ctrl` ID.
        *   Let's check: "S switch... 'ctrl': id of a SYNC". Yes.
        *   So, a synchronous bridge:
            - S1, S3 (top/bottom) controlled by SYNC1.
            - S2, S4 (top/bottom) controlled by SYNC2.
            - This is complex to time.

    *   *Topology 3: Zener-Clamped FBR*
        *   The FBR failed S3 ($V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$). Adding a DZ33 Zener diode from `out` to `0` will clamp it to $\sim 3.3\text{ V}$.
        *   This doesn't help S2 or S4 ($V_{avg}$ too low).

    *   *Topology 4: Inductor-boosted interface (Buck-Boost or similar)*
        *   The prompt mentions "L-Cp inversion". Let's refine the SSHI approach.
        *   Piezo $\to$ Switch/Inductor flipping $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage.
        *   Flip circuit: $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$, $S$ between $n1$ and $pzn$. $S$ is controlled by $SYNC$.
        *   Rectifier: Diode bridge from $pzp/pzn$ to $out$.
        *   Wait, if the flip circuit is in parallel, it doesn't provide the energy; it just prepares the piezo voltage. The energy still has to be extracted.
        *   A simpler version of SSHI:
            Piezo is $C_p$.
            $L$ and $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
            At $V_{max}$, $S$ closes, $C_p$ and $L$ resonate, $V_{C_p}$ becomes $-V_{C_p}$.
            Meanwhile, the current is rectified.
            Wait, the most efficient way is often a "Parallel-SSHI" or a simple "Synchronous Rectifier".

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Charge Extraction (SCE)** or a **modified SSHI**.
    *   Actually, look at the FBR again. It fails S2 and S4. It needs more voltage.
    *   If we use an inductor to flip the voltage, we effectively double the voltage across the rectifier diodes (or reduce the effect of the diode drop relative to the peak).
    *   *Circuit Proposal 1 (SSHI-FBR):*
        - Piezo terminals $pzp, pzn$.
        - Flipping circuit: Inductor $L_1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$, Switch $S_1$ from $n1$ to $pzn$.
        - SYNC $G_1$ controls $S_1$ at both edges.
        - Standard FBR: $D_1[pzp, out]$, $D_2[pzn, out]$, $D_3[0, pzp]$, $D_4[0, pzn]$.
        - Storage: $C_{out}$ at $out$.
        - Clamp: $D_{zener}[0, out]$ (DZ33).

    *   *Circuit Proposal 2 (Synchronous Rectifier - Half Bridge):*
        - Instead of a full bridge, use a switch and a diode to reduce drops.
        - But a full bridge is more robust for AC.

    *   *Circuit Proposal 3 (Simple SSHI without full bridge):*
        - Just use a switch to connect the piezo to the output at the peaks.
        - $pzp \to S_1 \to out$
        - $pzn \to S_2 \to out$
        - This is effectively a synchronous rectifier.
        - $S_1$ closes at positive peak, $S_2$ at negative peak.
        - To prevent backflow, we'd need diodes or precise timing.
        - Let's try: $pzp \to S_1 \to out$ (S1 closes at pos peak), $pzn \to S_2 \to out$ (S2 closes at neg peak).
        - This is very efficient.
        - $S_1$: ctrl=G1, edges=pos, phase=0.
        - $S_2$: ctrl=G2, edges=neg, phase=0.
        - $C_{out}$ at $out$.
        - Zener clamp $D_{zener}[0, out]$.

    *   $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$.
    *   The load $R_L$ can be as low as $150\text{ k}\Omega$.
    *   Current $I_{load} = 1.8\text{ V} / 150\text{ k}\Omega = 12\text{ \mu A}$.
    *   The piezo $I_p = 50\text{ \mu A}$ (peak).
    *   Energy per cycle $E \approx 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 = 25\text{ nF} \cdot (3.2)^2 \approx 256\text{ nJ}$.
    *   At $100\text{ Hz}$, Power $P = 256\text{ nJ} \cdot 100\text{ Hz} = 25.6\text{ \mu W}$.
    *   Load power $P_{load} = 1.8^2 / 150\text{ k}\Omega \approx 21.6\text{ \mu W}$.
    *   It's tight. Diode drops (0.25V each) in a bridge (0.5V total) reduce the available voltage significantly: $(3.2 - 0.5) = 2.7\text{ V}$.
    *   $P \approx 25\text{ nF} \cdot (2.7)^2 \cdot 100 \approx 18.2\text{ \mu W}$.
    *   This explains why FBR fails S2. Synchronous rectification (switches) will eliminate the $0.5\text{ V}$ drop.

    *   *Structure 1: Synchronous Rectifier (Direct Switch)*
        - SYNC G1: edges=pos, phase=0, ton=... (transfers charge from Cp to Cout)
        - S1: [pzp, out], ctrl=G1
        - SYNC G2: edges=neg, phase=0, ton=...
        - S2: [pzn, out], ctrl=G2
        - C1: [out, 0]
        - D1: [0, out], model=DZ33 (clamp)
        - This is very efficient. $t_{on}$ needs to be optimized.

    *   *Structure 2: SSHI with FBR (Voltage Boost)*
        - L1: [pzp, n1], value=...
        - S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl=G1
        - SYNC G1: edges=both, phase=0, ton=...
        - D1: [pzp, out], model=DSCH
        - D2: [pzn, out], model=DSCH
        - D3: [0, pzp], model=DSCH
        - D4: [0, pzn], model=DSCH
        - C1: [out, 0]
        - D5: [0, out], model=DZ33
        - SSHI increases the voltage across the bridge, helping with S2/S4.

    *   *Structure 3: Synchronous Half-Bridge with Inductor (Boost)*
        - Use an inductor to boost the voltage.
        - $pzp \to L1 \to S1 \to out$
        - $pzn \to L1 \to S2 \to out$ (wait, only one inductor $L1$?)
        - Better: $pzp \to L1 \to S1 \to out$, $pzn \to L2 \to S2 \to out$.
        - This might be overkill.

    *   Let's refine Structure 1 (Synchronous Rectifier).
        - S1: [pzp, out], ctrl=G1
        - S2: [pzn, out], ctrl=G2
        - G1: edges=pos, phase=0
        - G2: edges=neg, phase=0
        - C1: [out, 0]
        - Dz: [0, out], model=DZ33
        - To prevent $C_{out}$ from discharging back into $C_p$ when the switches are open, we rely on $R_{off}=1\text{ G}\Omega$. But when the switch is *closed*, if $V_{out} > V_{pzp}$, current flows back.
        - We need the switches to close only when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.
        - With $V_{oc}=3.2\text{ V}$ and $V_{out} \approx 1.8\text{--}3.3\text{ V}$, this is possible.
        - However, at $V_{out} = 3.3\text{ V}$, the switches will only conduct for a tiny fraction of the peak.
        - Let's add diodes in series with switches to be safe, or just rely on the SYNC's $t_{on}$. $t_{on}$ is very small ($10\text{--}100\text{ \mu s}$), which limits backflow.

    *   Let's refine Structure 2 (SSHI + Bridge).
        - This is a classic, proven topology.
        - Flipping circuit increases $V_{pzp}$ peaks.
        - Rectifier harvests it.
        - Zener clamps it.

    *   Wait, if I use a SYNC rectifier (Structure 1), it's like a bridge but with switches.
        If $V_{out}$ is $2\text{ V}$ and $V_{pzp}$ peaks at $3.2\text{ V}$, the switch conducts.
        If $V_{pzp}$ drops to $0\text{ V}$, the switch is open.
        This is very efficient.

    *   Let's try:
        1.  **Sync-Rect**: S1[pzp, out], S2[pzn, out], G1(pos), G2(neg), C1[out, 0], Dz[0, out].
        2.  **SSHI-Bridge**: L1[pzp, n1], S1[n1, pzn], G1(both), D1-4(bridge), C1[out, 0], Dz[0, out].
        3.  **Zener-FBR**: (Reference but with Zener) - actually, let's try a **Synchronous-Switching-Half-Bridge** (S1[pzp, out], D1[pzn, out], etc. - no, that's not right).
        Let's try **Parallel-SSHI** logic:
        - $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with $C_p$.
        - $D1$ from $pzp$ to $out$, $D2$ from $pzn$ to $out$. (Half bridge).
        - No, a full bridge is safer.

    *   Let's stick to:
        1.  `SyncRect`: High efficiency, removes diode drops.
        2.  `SSHI_FBR`: Voltage enhancement via $L-C_p$ resonance.
        3.  `SyncHalfBridge`: S1[pzp, out], S2[pzn, out] but with a capacitor and a zener. (Actually, the same as SyncRect). Let's try a different one: `InductorBoost`. $pzp \to L1 \to S1 \to out$, $pzn \to L1 \to S2 \to out$. No, that won't work.
        Let's try `DiodeHalfBridge` with $L-C_p$ flip.
        $L1$ [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (both), D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], C1 [out, 0], Dz [0, out].
        Wait, D1 and D2 alone are not a full bridge. D3 and D4 (to ground) are needed to handle the negative cycle of the piezo.
        Correct SSHI-FBR:
        L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1(both)
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]
        C1 [out, 0], Dz [0, out]

    *   `SyncRect`:
        S1 [pzp, out], G1 (pos)
        S2 [pzn, out], G2 (neg)
        C1 [out, 0]
        Dz [0, out] (DZ33)
        This has no diodes, so it's very efficient. $V_{out}$ can reach $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$.

    *   `SSHI_FBR`:
        L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (both)
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]
        C1 [out, 0]
        Dz [0, out] (DZ33)
        This enhances the voltage, helping S2/S4.

    *   `SSHI_SyncRect`:
        L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (both)
        S2 [pzp, out], G2 (pos)
        S3 [pzn, out], G3 (neg)
        C1 [out, 0]
        Dz [0, out]
        Wait, I only have 2 SYNC controllers.
        G1 (both) for flipping, G2 (both) for rectification?
        S2 [pzp, out] and S3 [pzn, out].
        G2: edges=both.
        Wait, if G2 is "both", then $S2$ and $S3$ both close at the same time? No, that would short $pzp$ and $pzn$.
        G2 must be "pos" for S2 and G3 must be "neg" for S3.
        But I only have 2 SYNCs.
        So I can have G1 (flipping) and G2 (rectifying).
        If G2 is "both", I can't use it for both S2 and S3 unless I have two different SYNCs.
        Let's use G1 for flipping (both) and G2 for S2 (pos). S3 is a diode.
        Or just stick to `SyncRect` and `SSHI_FBR`.

    *   Let's try a third one: `ChargePump-like` or `Half-Bridge Sync`.
        S1 [pzp, out], G1 (pos)
        D1 [pzn, out]
        D2 [pzp, 0]
        D3 [pzn, 0]
        C1 [out, 0]
        Dz [0, out]
        This is a hybrid.

    *   Let's re-evaluate the `SyncRect`. It's very simple and should be very efficient.
        G1: pos, G2: neg.
        S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out].
        This effectively replaces the whole bridge.
        Wait, the bridge also has diodes to ground. In `SyncRect`, when $S1$ is closed, $pzp$ is connected to $out$. What happens to $pzn$? It's just floating (connected to 1GOhm).
        Is this okay?
        In a full bridge:
        Pos peak: $pzp \to out$, $pzn \to 0$.
        Neg peak: $pzn \to out$, $pzp \to 0$.
        In `SyncRect`:
        Pos peak: $pzp \to out$, $pzn$ is floating.
        Neg peak: $pzn \to out$, $pzp$ is floating.
        This is slightly different but should still work. The "floating" side just doesn't discharge.

    *   Let's refine the `SyncRect` to be a full synchronous bridge if possible.
        S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out]
        S3 [pzp, 0], S4 [pzn, 0]
        G1: edges=pos (S1 and S4)
        G2: edges=neg (S2 and S3)
        Now it's a full synchronous bridge!
        Pos peak: S1 and S4 closed $\to pzp \to out, pzn \to 0$.
        Neg peak: S2 and S3 closed $\to pzn \to out, pzp \to 0$.
        This is the most efficient rectifier possible.

    *   **Proposal 1: `FullSyncBridge`**
        - S1 [pzp, out], S4 [pzn, 0], ctrl=G1, G1(edges=pos, phase=0)
        - S2 [pzn, out], S3 [pzp, 0], ctrl=G2, G2(edges=neg, phase=0)
        - C1 [out, 0]
        - Dz [0, out] (DZ33)

    *   **Proposal 2: `SSHI_FBR`**
        - L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], ctrl=G1, G1(edges=both, phase=0)
        - D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (DSCH)
        - C1 [out, 0]
        - Dz [0, out] (DZ33)

    *   **Proposal 3: `SSHI_SyncBridge`**
        - L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], ctrl=G1, G1(edges=both, phase=0)
        - S2 [pzp, out], S4 [pzn, 0], ctrl=G2, G2(edges=pos, phase=0)
